ops.title: no durable breadcrumb survives a daemon that fails to start
ops.description:
A daemon whose Start fails publishes PhaseFailed — serve.go:259-261 calls rt.fail(), which
is r.publish(wire.PhaseFailed) (serve.go:564-566) — and the wire client does surface that as
a typed error: WaitReady returns &RuntimeFailedError{Snapshot: snapshot} on PhaseFailed
(internal/wire/client.go:331-347). That path is sound for a client already attached.

Nobody is attached. Serve falls straight into runShutdownLadder (serve.go:272), whose first
stage is StageIntake: stage(StageIntake, server.CloseIntake() == nil) (serve.go:332), and
CloseIntake closes the listener (internal/wire/server.go:520-530). The phase stream that
carried PhaseFailed lived on that socket, so the signal dies with it. Every later dial can
only ever answer ErrAbsent — "daemonkit: no daemon is listening" (errors.go:21) — which is
literally true and diagnostically useless.

Nothing durable catches the signal on the way past. The owner record carries no failure
field (internal/proc/owner.go:16-22 is PID, Start, Boot, Generation, Build), and
paths/paths.go has no status or last-error path at all — DBPath, SocketPath, LogPath,
HTTPInfoPath, ChannelSetupMarkerPath, the lock and subject and turn paths, and nothing else.

Net effect for an operator: the error names a dead socket while the real cause is only in
the daemon's own log, which nothing in the client API points at. This is exactly the
"actionable error" gap cc-pool's bug 7648cd1 asked for — there the surfaced error was
"daemonkit: no daemon is listening: wire: dial: ... no such file or directory" while the
real cause, a catalog generation mismatch, was only ever written to holder.log.

ops.text: After a Start failure, a client that dials afterwards can name the failure — not only ErrAbsent.
The failure reason outlives the listener teardown: it is recorded durably before runShutdownLadder closes intake, and a later process can read it without a session.
The operator-facing error either carries the cause or names where it is (the daemon log path); a dead-socket message alone does not satisfy this.
A test proves the whole arc: a daemon whose Start returns an error, Serve returning, then a fresh client observing the recorded failure instead of a bare ErrAbsent.
